overview: This unit introduces discrete mathematics (Diskrete Mathematik) and the precise formulation of mathematical concepts. It covers propositions (Aussagen), logical connectives (Junktoren), quantifiers (Quantoren), truth tables (Wahrheitstabellen), and logical equivalence (logische Gleichwertigkeit). Propositional forms describe values for which a condition holds; their solution sets can be determined, and general claims can be refuted by counterexamples.

entries.short: Discrete mathematics studies distinguishable objects, sets, systems, and structures.
entries.explanation: It treats objects as individual elements and studies the relationships and structures among them. Its topics include graph theory, combinatorics, logic, and algebra.
entries.example: A network of individual nodes and connections can be studied as a discrete structure.
entries.heading: 1. Worum geht es?

entries.short: Discrete means considering individual, distinguishable elements; continuous means modeling intermediate values without gaps.
entries.explanation: A discrete model treats possible objects individually. A continuous model allows intermediate values without gaps; in classical physics, space and time are often modeled this way. Which description is appropriate depends on the question.
entries.example: The number of people is discrete, while a modeled duration can be continuous.
pitfalls: A continuous model is a modeling assumption, not automatically an exact description of reality.
entries.heading: 1. Worum geht es?

entries.short: A set is countable if its elements can be numbered using the natural numbers.
entries.explanation: For a countable set, the elements can be listed in sequence; finite sets are also considered countable. The sets \(\mathbb{N}\), \(\mathbb{Z}\), and \(\mathbb{Q}\) are countable, whereas \(\mathbb{R}\) is uncountable. Countability does not mean that there are no other elements between any two elements.
entries.example: For example, the integers can be listed as \(0, 1, -1, 2, -2, 3, -3, \ldots\).
pitfalls: The density of the rational numbers in the real numbers does not make \(\mathbb{Q}\) uncountable.
entries.heading: 1. Worum geht es?

entries.short: The course covers foundations, graph theory, combinatorics, logic, and algebra.
entries.explanation: The foundations include informal logic, sets, functions, relations, cardinality, pseudocode, and data types. Graph theory studies nodes, edges, and weighted graphs; combinatorics counts sets and supports discrete probability and runtime estimates. Logic deals with the syntax and semantics of propositional formulas, while algebra studies structures such as groups.
entries.heading: Themen der Vorlesung

entries.short: Graph theory studies graphs made up of nodes and edges.
entries.explanation: A graph describes relationships among objects: the objects are called nodes, and the relationships are called edges. In a weighted graph, each edge also has a value assigned to it. Graphs can model data structures, routes, or social networks, for example.
entries.example: In a road network, intersections can be nodes and roads can be edges; road length can serve as the edge weight.
entries.heading: Themen der Vorlesung

entries.short: Unambiguity means that an expression can be interpreted clearly and as intended.
entries.explanation: Mathematical statements and concepts should have a meaning that can be determined. Ambiguity arises when a sentence allows multiple readings, for example because it is unclear what a modifier refers to. Unambiguous wording makes it possible to assess statements reliably and reason with them.
entries.example: “I saw a man on the hill with a telescope” leaves open whether the man or the speaker had the telescope.
pitfalls: A grammatically correct formulation is not necessarily unambiguous.
entries.heading: 2. Eindeutigkeit und Aussagen

entries.short: Parentheses and punctuation help structure expressions unambiguously.
entries.explanation: Parentheses show which parts of an expression belong together and how they are nested. Correctly nested parenthesized expressions belong to the Dyck language. This structure helps make mathematical and formal expressions unambiguous.
entries.example: The sequence `(()())` is correctly nested, while the sequence `(()` is not fully closed.
pitfalls: Having the same number of opening and closing parentheses is not enough; their order must also be correct.
entries.heading: 2. Eindeutigkeit und Aussagen

entries.short: A definition establishes the meaning of a concept in a particular context.
entries.explanation: A definition determines how a concept is used within a specified context. This allows concepts to be understood consistently in statements and proofs. A definition establishes a meaning rather than proving a claim about the subject matter.
entries.example: A graph is a structure made up of nodes and edges.
pitfalls: A definition should not be confused with a theorem whose truth must be proved.
entries.heading: 2. Eindeutigkeit und Aussagen

entries.short: A logical expression is satisfiable if there is an assignment under which it is true.
entries.explanation: An assignment gives truth values to propositional variables. A propositional expression is satisfiable if at least one assignment makes the entire expression true. Satisfiability does not require the expression to be true under every assignment.
entries.example: The expression \(A \land B\) is satisfiable because it is true when both \(A\) and \(B\) are true.
pitfalls: Satisfiable does not mean that an expression is true under every assignment.
entries.heading: 2. Eindeutigkeit und Aussagen

entries.short: A proposition is the content of a declarative sentence.
entries.explanation: A proposition asserts something that can be true or false. Questions and commands are not propositions in this sense. Propositions can be combined into compound propositions using logical connectives.
entries.example: “The number 4 is even” is a true proposition.
pitfalls: An expression with a free variable has no fixed truth value until a value is assigned to the variable or it is quantified.
entries.heading: 2. Eindeutigkeit und Aussagen

entries.short: Logical connectives combine propositions into compound propositions or modify a single proposition.
entries.explanation: Logical connectives include conjunction \(\land\) (“and”), disjunction \(\lor\) (“or”), negation \(\neg\) (“not”), implication \(\Rightarrow\), equivalence \(\Leftrightarrow\), and exclusive or \(\oplus\). The propositional “or” is inclusive: \(A \lor B\) is also true when both propositions are true. Negation is unary; each of the other connectives listed combines two propositions.
entries.example: If \(A\) means “It is raining” and \(B\) means “The road is wet,” then \(A \land B\) expresses that both are true.
pitfalls: Inclusive \(\lor\) must be distinguished from exclusive \(\oplus\).
Negation \(\neg\) does not combine two propositions.
entries.heading: 3. Logische Ausdrücke

entries.short: Quantifiers specify which objects a propositional form is meant to apply to.
entries.explanation: \(\forall x\,P(x)\) means “for all \(x\), \(P(x)\) holds,” and \(\exists x\,P(x)\) means “there is an \(x\) for which \(P(x)\) holds.” \(\nexists x\,P(x)\) means there is no \(x\) for which \(P(x)\) holds. The domain of discourse must be specified so it is clear which objects are meant.
entries.example: \(\forall x\in\mathbb{R}: x^2\geq 0\) states that the square of every real number is nonnegative.
pitfalls: Without a specified domain, it may be unclear what the quantifier ranges over.
entries.heading: 3. Logische Ausdrücke

entries.short: “All A are B” and “All B are C” imply “All A are C.”
entries.explanation: A syllogism is a form of reasoning in which two general statements support a third. Formally, \(\forall x(A(x)\Rightarrow B(x))\) and \(\forall x(B(x)\Rightarrow C(x))\) entail \(\forall x(A(x)\Rightarrow C(x))\). The names of the groups are irrelevant to the validity of the inference.
entries.example: All Bandersnatches are Borogoves; all Borogoves are slithy; therefore, all Bandersnatches are slithy.
pitfalls: The conclusion follows only on the assumption that both premises hold.
entries.heading: Ein Schlussbeispiel: Syllogismus

entries.short: A truth table shows the truth values of an expression for every assignment of its propositional variables.
entries.explanation: For two propositions \(A\) and \(B\), there are four assignments, all of which appear in a complete table. The lecture notes use \(w\) for true and \(f\) for false. For \(n\) propositional variables, there are \(2^n\) possible assignments.
entries.example: For \(A\Rightarrow B\), only the assignment \(A=w\), \(B=f\) is false.
pitfalls: Omitting an assignment makes the table incomplete.
entries.heading: Eine Wahrheitstabelle für die Junktoren

entries.short: A binary connective is symmetric if swapping the propositions does not change its truth value.
entries.explanation: Conjunction, disjunction, equivalence, and exclusive or are symmetric: swapping \(A\) and \(B\) leaves the truth value unchanged. Implication is asymmetric in this sense because its direction matters. Negation is unary and does not belong to these binary connectives.
entries.example: When \(A=w\) and \(B=f\), \(A\Rightarrow B\) is false, but \(B\Rightarrow A\) is true.
pitfalls: Here, “asymmetric” refers to the possibility that swapping the two propositions changes the truth value.
entries.heading: Eine Wahrheitstabelle für die Junktoren

entries.short: \(A\Rightarrow B\) means “if \(A\), then \(B\)” and is false only when \(A\) is true and \(B\) is false.
entries.explanation: In an implication, \(A\) is the premise and \(B\) is the conclusion. The expression is true if \(A\) is false or \(B\) is true. Direction matters: \(A\Rightarrow B\) and \(B\Rightarrow A\) generally have different truth values.
entries.example: “If a number is divisible by 4, then it is even” is a true implication.
pitfalls: A true implication does not assert that its premise is actually satisfied.
entries.heading: Eine Wahrheitstabelle für die Junktoren

entries.example: “If it is raining, the road is wet” and “It is not raining or the road is wet” are logically equivalent.
pitfalls: Equivalence requires matching truth values under every assignment, not merely similar wording.
entries.heading: Gleichbedeutende Aussagen

entries.short: An open sentence contains a variable and becomes a proposition when a value is substituted for it.
entries.explanation: The truth value of an open sentence depends on the value substituted for its variable. The domain must be specified because it determines which values are considered. After a specific value is substituted, the expression is true or false.
entries.example: For \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), substituting \(x=2\) into \(x^2=4\) gives the true proposition \(2^2=4\).
pitfalls: An open sentence with a free variable has no fixed truth value yet.
entries.heading: 4. Aussageformen und Lösungsmengen

entries.short: The solution set of an open sentence contains all values in the domain under consideration for which it is true.
entries.explanation: For an open sentence \(P(x)\) with domain \(D\), the solution set is \(L=\{x\in D\mid P(x)\text{ is true}\}\). It may contain a single value, several values, the entire domain, or no values at all. The domain must be known to determine the solution set.
entries.example: For \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), the solution set of \(x^2=4\) is \(L=\{-2,2\}\).
pitfalls: The solution set may change when a different domain is considered.
entries.heading: 4. Aussageformen und Lösungsmengen

entries.short: A counterexample is a case that refutes a general claim.
entries.explanation: For a claim meant to hold for every value in a domain, one value for which it is false suffices to refute its general validity. The value must satisfy the claim’s assumptions and show that the stated conclusion does not hold. A counterexample does not automatically prove another general statement.
entries.example: For \(x=-2\), \(x^2=4\) is true but \(x=2\) is false; therefore, \(x^2=4\Rightarrow x=2\) does not hold for all real \(x\).
pitfalls: A case in which a claim holds does not prove that it holds in general.
entries.heading: 4. Aussageformen und Lösungsmengen

entries.short: A Venn diagram illustrates sets and their relationships using overlapping regions.
entries.explanation: In a Venn diagram, circles can represent sets. Overlapping regions show shared elements; other regions show elements that belong to only one of the sets shown. Open sentences can also be illustrated with such diagrams.
entries.example: The overlapping region for two sets \(A\) and \(B\) represents their intersection \(A\cap B\).
pitfalls: A diagram illustrates relationships but does not automatically replace a formal proof.
entries.heading: 4. Aussageformen und Lösungsmengen
